newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Zaire threatens to expel Rwanda, Burundi refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire threatens to expel Rwanda, Burundi refugees.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Zaire, lashing out at its critics, said on Thursday it would expel more than a million refugees from the ethnic conflicts in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi if they did not return home willingly.
The vast central African country suspended an attempt to forcibly repatriate Rwandans last August, following an international outcry.

But Foreign Minister Kititwa Tumansi told the U.N. General Assembly in New York that his country had suffered from the influx of refugees and received no international help. He signalled that the government's patience was running out.
"Zaire is always prepared to cooperate with ... Rwanda and Burundi ... to ensure the voluntary and dignified return of refugees," he said.
"Failing which ... Zaire will have no choice but to proceed to enforced and unconditional return of refugees to their countries of origin."
Zaire's relations with Rwanda have been poor since 1994 but have worsened in the past month, with demonstrations in Kinshasa calling for the expulsion of the refugees.

An estimated 1.1 million Hutu refugees are afraid to return to Rwanda where Hutus are blamed for the genocide of up to 1 million minority Tutsis or Hutu moderates in 1994. There are also refugees from the conflict in Burundi.
"Zaire will never accept the de facto transformation of its territoy to a Hutu-land ... those who are thinking of that should forget it," Kititwa said.
"Zaire does not accept and will never again accept to serve as a scapegoat for anyone (and) will defend by all means the security of its population and its borders."
Most of the refugees are concentrated in eastern Zaire. Kinshasa says they create insecurity, destroy the economy and the environment and drive Zaireans from their land.
President Mobutu Sese Seko has been under pressure from the United States and European powers to speed up the promised transition to democracy.
Mobutu, who seized power in a 1965 coup, ruled the country with an iron fist for a quarter of a century but introduced the beginnings of a multi-party system in 1990.
Nevertheless, Zaire's transition has lagged well behind that of other states in the region and human rights groups have continued to criticise the government.
Kititwa said such accusations were "unfounded and unwarranted."
"Zaire wishes to reaffirm ... that the democratization of its political system is irreversible," he said. "Zaire has nothing to hide."
According to Zaire's transitional constitution, which was extended again last July, presidential and parliamentary elections must be held by July 1997.
The election commission said the elections are still on course for May but has put back a voter census and constitutional referendum.
Main donors -- former colonial power Belgium, France, and the United States -- have cut all but humanitarian aid in protest at human rights abuses and delays in the transition.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is due to visit Africa next week but will not go to Zaire.
